questions.q: A 6-week-old is brought for review. Birth weight was 3.2 kg; current weight is 3.0 kg. Feeding is reported as 'on demand' but wet nappies are only 2/day. The nurse’s priority is to:
options: Reassure that weight loss after birth always continues for 2 months
Assess feeding technique/intake thoroughly and escalate for failure to thrive / dehydration risk
Advise switching to adult food immediately
questions.explanation: Ongoing weight below birth weight with few wet nappies suggests inadequate intake or illness — needs full assessment and action.

questions.q: Which finding in a 9-month-old is most concerning and needs prompt review?
options: No social smile ever observed and no interest in people
questions.explanation: Absent social engagement by this age is a red flag for developmental or social-emotional concern.

questions.q: A mother asks when to start complementary foods for a healthy term breastfed infant. The best evidence-based reply is:
options: Around 6 months, while continuing breastfeeding, starting iron-rich soft foods
questions.explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding to about 6 months, then complementary foods with continued breastfeeding.

questions.q: A 14-month-old’s weight has fallen across two major centile lines since 6 months. The priority nursing action is to:
options: Ignore if the child looks active in clinic once
Take a detailed diet/illness/social history and ensure urgent clinical review for faltering growth
Start adult portion sizes immediately without assessment
questions.explanation: Crossing centiles downward needs systematic evaluation of intake, illness and environment.

questions.q: Which sign in severe acute malnutrition needs the most urgent recognition?
options: Bilateral pitting oedema, lethargy, or inability to complete a feed (complicated SAM)
questions.explanation: Oedema, lethargy and poor feeding mark complicated SAM requiring urgent care.

questions.q: A 2-year-old has barky cough, hoarse cry, and stridor at rest. The priority is to:
options: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor immediately
Keep the child calm, give oxygen if hypoxic, and escalate for croup management — avoid agitating the airway
Force the child flat on the bed
Give oral fluids only and send home without review
questions.explanation: Stridor at rest is moderate–severe croup; keep calm and treat; do not instrument the throat casually.

questions.q: A 6-month-old with bronchiolitis has RR 68, oxygen saturation 88% in air, and poor feeding. The nurse’s priority is to:
options: Support airway/oxygen as protocol, minimise handling, and ensure urgent medical review
Feed large volumes quickly while supine
questions.explanation: Hypoxia, tachypnoea and poor feeding indicate need for oxygen and hospital-level care.

questions.q: Which child with asthma needs the most immediate intervention?
options: Mild wheeze, speaking full sentences, saturations 97%
Silent chest, exhaustion, saturations 90%, able to say only one word
Night cough only, normal daytime activity
Wheeze that responds fully to one bronchodilator dose
questions.explanation: Silent chest and exhaustion signal life-threatening asthma.

questions.q: A toddler swallowed a small battery. He is drooling and refusing solids. The priority is to:
options: Keep NPO, avoid inducing vomiting, and arrange urgent emergency/ENT evaluation for button battery
questions.explanation: Button batteries can cause severe oesophageal injury within hours — urgent removal pathway.

questions.q: A 4-year-old with pneumonia is on oxygen. Which observation must be reported immediately?
options: Sudden increase in work of breathing and desaturation to 85%
questions.explanation: Worsening respiratory distress and hypoxia need immediate escalation.

questions.q: Teaching for home nebuliser/inhaler use is effective when the caregiver says:
options: I stop the inhaler as soon as the child feels better mid-course without advice
I use a spacer for the MDI, give doses as prescribed, and seek care if the child is not improving
I share the same inhaler mouthpiece with siblings without cleaning
I only treat after the child turns blue
questions.explanation: Correct device technique and clear escalation advice are essential.

questions.q: A child with suspected epiglottitis is sitting forward, drooling, and toxic-looking. The nurse should:
options: Lie the child flat and inspect the throat with a spatula
Do not agitate, keep in preferred position, give oxygen as tolerated, and call for urgent airway-capable help
Send to the waiting area alone
questions.explanation: Suspected epiglottitis is an airway emergency — no throat exam by unprepared staff.

questions.q: A 6-week-old has temperature 38.5°C, is irritable, and feeds poorly. The priority is to:
options: Advise only tepid sponging at home for 3 days
Treat as possible serious bacterial infection — urgent assessment and septic work-up pathway
questions.explanation: Fever in young infants is high risk; prompt medical evaluation is required.

questions.q: Which febrile child is highest priority for immediate review?
options: 9-month-old lethargic, non-blanching rash, and cold hands
School-age child with fever day 1 and good oral intake
questions.explanation: Lethargy plus purpuric rash suggests meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.

questions.q: A child is on IV antibiotics for meningitis. Which nursing assessment is most critical ongoing?
options: Neurological status, fontanelle (if open), seizures, and fluid balance
questions.explanation: Neuro observations and complications of raised ICP/seizures drive monitoring.

questions.q: Caregiver teaching after a simple febrile seizure should include:
options: The child will definitely develop epilepsy
Most simple febrile seizures are self-limiting; protect airway during the event, seek care for prolonged/focal seizures, and treat the cause of fever
questions.explanation: Education reduces fear while highlighting when emergency care is needed.

questions.q: A child with measles is admitted. Priority nursing measures include:
options: Airborne/appropriate isolation, vitamin A as protocol, eye care, and monitoring for complications
questions.explanation: Measles needs isolation, supportive care and complication surveillance.

questions.q: Which statement about oral rehydration for diarrhoea is correct?
options: ORS is withheld if the child is thirsty
ORS is first-line for most dehydration; continue breastfeeding; escalate if severe dehydration or shock
IV fluids are required for every watery stool
Antibiotics are always needed for watery diarrhoea
questions.explanation: ORS and continued feeding are central; severe disease needs IV and higher care.

questions.q: A child with diarrhoea has sunken eyes, skin pinch going back slowly, and drinks eagerly. This is best classified as:
options: Some dehydration — needs ORS plan under observation
Severe dehydration only if weight is normal
questions.explanation: WHO some-dehydration signs guide ORS treatment plans.

questions.q: A child with severe dehydration is lethargic and unable to drink. The priority is to:
options: IV (or intraosseous) fluids urgently per protocol and continuous monitoring
Wait for laboratory results before any fluid
questions.explanation: Severe dehydration with inability to drink requires parenteral fluids.

questions.q: An infant with a known VSD is sweaty, tachypnoeic, and poor at feeding. The nurse suspects:
options: Possible heart failure — prioritise feeding support, oxygen if needed, and medical review
questions.explanation: Effort intolerance with feeds suggests cardiac failure in infants with shunts.

questions.q: During a tet spell, the priority nursing action is to:
options: Lay the infant flat and start vigorous crying encouragement
Knee–chest position, calm the child, oxygen, and call for help / follow protocol
Give a large bottle feed first
Ignore until the spell ends alone always
questions.explanation: Knee–chest and calming reduce right-to-left shunting in hypercyanotic spells.

questions.q: Before giving digoxin to a child, the nurse must:
options: Give it with any heart rate
Check apical pulse for a full minute and hold if below the ordered threshold; check recent electrolytes if relevant
Crush and mix into a full litre of milk always
Skip assessment if the child is asleep
questions.explanation: Digoxin requires rate check and caution with electrolytes.

questions.q: A child post-cardiac catheterisation has a cool, pulseless foot on the catheter side. The priority is to:
questions.explanation: Limb ischaemia after catheterisation is an emergency.

questions.q: A toddler has a generalised seizure lasting 8 minutes. After protecting the head and positioning, the next priority is to:
options: Time the seizure, maintain airway, give oxygen if available, and prepare rescue medication per protocol if prolonged
Give oral fluids during the seizure
questions.explanation: Prolonged seizures need airway support and emergency antiseizure treatment pathways.

questions.q: Which post-ictal finding needs urgent review?
options: Sleepiness for 20 minutes after a brief seizure
Persistent focal weakness or failure to return toward baseline mental status
questions.explanation: Todd’s paresis lasting unusually or altered consciousness needs evaluation for complications.

questions.q: A child with suspected raised ICP should be positioned:
options: Head midline, head of bed elevated ~30° if not contraindicated
questions.explanation: Neutral head elevation supports venous drainage.

questions.q: A 3-year-old has acute ataxia after a viral illness. The nurse should:
options: Ensure safety, full assessment, and medical review — post-infectious cerebellar ataxia is a diagnosis of exclusion
questions.explanation: Acute ataxia needs careful evaluation to exclude serious causes.

questions.q: A 4-week-old has progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting and a palpable olive mass. The nurse anticipates:
options: Evaluation for pyloric stenosis — fluid/electrolyte correction and surgical referral
questions.explanation: Projectile non-bilious vomiting with olive mass is classic pyloric stenosis.

questions.q: An infant has bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. The priority is to:
options: Reassure that bilious vomiting is always normal
NPO, IV access, urgent surgical review — bilious vomiting is obstruction until proven otherwise
questions.explanation: Bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.

questions.q: A 10-month-old has intermittent severe crying, drawing up legs, and currant-jelly stool. The nurse suspects:
questions.explanation: Intermittent pain and currant-jelly stool suggest intussusception.

questions.q: A child with gastroenteritis is ready for discharge when:
options: Hydration improved, taking ORS/feeds, urine output returning, and caregivers understand danger signs
questions.explanation: Stable hydration and caregiver education are discharge requirements.

questions.q: Post-op care after repair of tracheo-oesophageal fistula prioritises:
options: Early solid foods on day 0 always
Airway protection, careful feeding per protocol, and monitoring for aspiration/anastomotic problems
No suction ever under any order
questions.explanation: Airway and staged feeding are central after TOF repair.

questions.q: A child with nephrotic syndrome has sudden severe abdominal pain and fever. The nurse should:
questions.explanation: Nephrotic children are at risk of infection and clotting complications.

questions.q: Which assessment is most important in a child receiving IV fluids for dehydration?
options: Weight trends, hydration signs, urine output, and signs of overload
questions.explanation: Fluid therapy needs ongoing hydration and overload assessment.

questions.q: A child with acute glomerulonephritis has BP rising and headache. Priority action:
options: Report hypertension and neurological symptoms promptly — risk of complications
questions.explanation: Hypertension in AGN can cause encephalopathy; escalate early.

questions.q: A child with sickle cell disease has severe chest pain, fever, and tachypnoea. The priority is to:
options: Treat as simple muscle strain only
Oxygen, pain control, cultures/antibiotics as ordered — manage as acute chest syndrome pathway
questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome is life-threatening and needs urgent protocolised care.

questions.q: A haemophiliac child hits his head. He is drowsy. The nurse should:
options: Urgent assessment and factor replacement as protocol — intracranial bleed risk
Give IM injection in the buttock for pain
questions.explanation: Head injury in haemophilia requires urgent factor and evaluation.

questions.q: A child on chemotherapy has ANC 0.2 × 10⁹/L and a fever. Priority is to:
options: Urgent medical review and empiric antibiotics per febrile neutropenia protocol
questions.explanation: Febrile neutropenia is an emergency.

questions.q: Which nursing action is appropriate for a child with thrombocytopenia?
options: IM injections and rectal temperatures routinely
Avoid trauma, use soft toothbrush, monitor for bleeding
questions.explanation: Bleeding precautions are essential when platelets are low.

questions.q: A child with type 1 diabetes is sweaty, shaky, and confused. Capillary glucose is 2.4 mmol/L. The priority is to:
options: Give fast-acting carbohydrate (or glucagon/IV glucose if unable to swallow) per protocol
Ignore until the next scheduled check
questions.explanation: Hypoglycaemia is treated with glucose, not insulin.

questions.q: Teaching for sick-day management in childhood diabetes is correct when the caregiver says:
options: I stop insulin whenever the child is ill
I check glucose more often, never stop basal insulin without advice, and seek help for vomiting or persistent highs
I only use water and skip all insulin
questions.explanation: Illness needs more monitoring and planned insulin adjustment — not abrupt cessation.

questions.q: A child with DKA is on insulin infusion. Which finding needs the most urgent attention?
options: Gradual fall in glucose as expected
Sudden drop in consciousness or ECG changes from hypokalaemia
questions.explanation: Cerebral oedema risk and potassium shifts are major DKA hazards.

questions.q: A child in a cast complains of severe pain unrelieved by elevation and analgesia; toes are cool and dusky. The priority is to:
options: Reassure that pain is always normal
Apply ice tightly over the whole cast without review
questions.explanation: Pain out of proportion with neurovascular change is compartment syndrome until proven otherwise.

questions.q: Suspected non-accidental injury is suggested when:
options: History matches a single bruise on the shin of a walking toddler
Injuries are inconsistent with the history or developmental stage, or there are patterned burns/bruises
A reported fall in a mobile school-age child with one abrasion
questions.explanation: Inconsistency with history/development and patterned injuries raise safeguarding concern.

questions.q: Nursing priority when NAI is suspected includes:
options: Confronting parents aggressively in the corridor
Treat injuries, document carefully, and follow safeguarding reporting pathways
questions.explanation: Safety, accurate records and formal safeguarding processes are required.

questions.q: A child with a fracture is in traction. Which finding must be reported?
options: Loss of sensation or pulses distal to the injury
questions.explanation: Neurovascular compromise needs urgent action.

questions.q: A 5-day-old has yellow sclera, poor feeding, and is hard to rouse. The priority is to:
options: Urgent review for possible pathological jaundice / sepsis / metabolic disease
Advise sunlight only for a week at home
questions.explanation: Early jaundice with poor feeding and lethargy is not 'watch and wait'.

questions.q: Apnoea in a preterm neonate that does not respond to stimulation requires:
options: Airway support / PPV as trained and escalation
questions.explanation: Unresponsive apnoea needs ventilation support.

questions.q: A neonate has not passed meconium by 48 hours and has abdominal distension. The nurse should:
options: Report for evaluation of obstruction / Hirschsprung / other pathology
questions.explanation: Delayed meconium with distension needs investigation.

questions.q: A child with croup improves with nebulised adrenaline then worsens 2 hours later. The nurse should:
options: Continue observation — rebound can occur; escalate if stridor/distress returns
Give a large solid meal mid-distress
questions.explanation: Post-adrenaline observation is required because symptoms can return.

questions.q: Which immunisation teaching is appropriate?
options: Skip all vaccines if the child had a mild cold without fever once
Mild illness is not usually a reason to defer; discuss true contraindications with the clinician
Vaccines cause autism so refuse all
Only one vaccine is ever needed in life
questions.explanation: Mild intercurrent illness rarely contraindicates vaccination.

questions.q: A school-age child with asthma uses a preventer. Correct understanding is shown by:
options: Using the preventer only during attacks
Taking the preventer daily as prescribed and using the reliever for symptoms
Stopping preventer when playing sport always
questions.explanation: Preventers are maintenance therapy; relievers treat acute symptoms.

questions.q: Priority nursing diagnosis for a child in vaso-occlusive sickle crisis is often related to:
questions.explanation: Pain and ischaemia drive acute crisis care.

questions.q: A toddler is post-tonsillectomy and is swallowing repeatedly, pale, and tachycardic. The nurse suspects:
questions.explanation: Frequent swallowing after tonsillectomy can signal bleeding.

questions.q: Which fluid is generally preferred for ORS?
options: Plain water for severe dehydration instead of IV when the child cannot drink
questions.explanation: ORS has defined electrolyte composition; soft drinks are inappropriate as primary ORS.

questions.q: A child with burns to the face and singed nasal hairs is at greatest risk for:
questions.explanation: Inhalation injury risk requires airway vigilance.

questions.q: Pain assessment in a non-verbal toddler is best supported by:
options: Behavioural tools (e.g. FLACC) plus caregiver input
Assuming no pain if not crying at that second
questions.explanation: Observational scales are validated for young children.

questions.q: A child on long-term steroids is exposed to chickenpox. The nurse should:
options: Seek urgent advice — immunocompromised children may need prophylaxis/treatment pathways
questions.explanation: Varicella exposure on steroids can be serious.

questions.q: Which sign suggests dehydration is improving?
options: Persistent doughy skin and no tears
Improved alertness, moist mucous membranes, and urine output increasing
questions.explanation: Clinical hydration markers should trend toward normal.

questions.q: A 2-year-old with suspected foreign body aspiration who is coughing effectively should:
options: Be encouraged to keep coughing; intervene with protocol back blows/thrusts only if effective cough is lost
Be given water to 'wash it down' while cyanosed
questions.explanation: Effective cough is protective; interventions follow choking algorithms when cough becomes ineffective.

questions.q: Parent teaching for ORS is correct when they say:
options: I give ORS only once then stop
I give small frequent amounts as advised and continue breastfeeding
I stop ORS when diarrhoea is still present on day 1 always
questions.explanation: Frequent small ORS volumes improve tolerance.

questions.q: A child with meningitis is on droplet precautions. The nurse should:
options: Skip hand hygiene if gloves are used
Use appropriate PPE and hand hygiene; continue until cleared per policy
Leave the door open to the playroom always
questions.explanation: Transmission-based precautions protect other children and staff.

questions.q: Which infant feeding pattern is concerning?
options: 8–12 breastfeeds in 24 hours with regular wet nappies
Sleeping 6 hours between feeds on day 2 with few wet nappies and lethargy
questions.explanation: Long intervals with oliguria and lethargy in a newborn need review.

questions.q: A child with nephrotic syndrome is discharged. Priority teaching includes:
options: Stopping prednisolone when oedema improves without advice
Daily weights, infection precautions, medication adherence, and when to seek care
questions.explanation: Monitoring and infection awareness are central at home.

questions.q: During a febrile neutropenia admission, which nursing action is essential?
options: Strict hand hygiene, avoid unnecessary invasive procedures, monitor fever
Crowded ward bay without isolation consideration
questions.explanation: Infection prevention is critical when neutrophils are very low.

questions.q: A child has suspected appendicitis. Which action is inappropriate?
options: NPO and IV access as ordered
Giving analgesia as prescribed while awaiting review
Applying heat to the abdomen and giving a laxative to 'clear the blockage'
questions.explanation: Laxatives/heat can be harmful if appendicitis is present.

questions.q: Priority in paediatric burns first aid is to:
options: Cool with running water (as protocol), cover cleanly, assess airway and circulation
questions.explanation: Cool running water and airway/circulation assessment are first-line.

questions.q: A child with diabetes is found unresponsive. Glucose is not immediately available. The nurse should:
options: Treat as hypoglycaemia with glucagon/IV glucose per protocol if unable to take oral sugar
Force oral tablets into a closed airway
questions.explanation: Unresponsive hypoglycaemia needs parenteral glucose/glucagon.

questions.q: Which developmental approach helps a preschooler cope with a procedure?
options: Simple honest explanation, play demonstration, and parent presence when possible
Lying about pain ('it will not hurt at all') if it will
questions.explanation: Age-appropriate preparation reduces fear.

questions.q: A child with severe malaria is prostrate with delayed capillary refill. Priority is:
options: Emergency ABC support and urgent parenteral treatment pathway
Waiting for parasite count before any care
questions.explanation: Severe malaria is a medical emergency.

questions.q: Post-operative tonsillectomy diet teaching includes:
options: Cool soft diet, avoid trauma to the operative site, report bleeding
Using straws vigorously if advised against
questions.explanation: Soft diet and bleeding vigilance are standard.

questions.q: A 15-month-old is not walking and has low tone. The nurse should:
questions.explanation: Not walking by 15–18 months warrants assessment.

questions.q: Which oxygen delivery approach is often preferred for a distressed infant who needs moderate oxygen?
options: Asking the infant to hold a mask tightly alone
Appropriate age device (e.g. nasal prongs) with saturation targeting per protocol
questions.explanation: Device choice and saturation targets guide oxygen therapy.

questions.q: A caregiver reports the child had a brief seizure with fever, recovered fully, and is playful. Teaching should emphasise:
options: No need to ever seek care for fever again
Treat fever source, safety during seizures, and red flags (prolonged, focal, repeated, incomplete recovery)
Avoiding medical care for future fevers
questions.explanation: Safety-netting after febrile seizure is essential.

questions.q: A child with a tracheostomy develops sudden respiratory distress. First actions include:
options: Suction as indicated, check tube patency, oxygen, and call for help
Removing the tube without training or equipment ready
questions.explanation: Tube obstruction is a common cause of acute distress.

questions.q: Which finding in acute glomerulonephritis is expected?
options: Massive proteinuria with normal urine colour always
Painless bright red heavy bleeding only as in adult trauma
questions.explanation: AGN typically features cola urine, oliguria and hypertension.

questions.q: A child is receiving a blood transfusion and develops fever, chills, and back pain. Priority is to:
options: Stop the transfusion, keep IV line with normal saline, and notify the clinician
Ignore if BP is normal once
questions.explanation: Suspected transfusion reaction → stop transfusion and escalate.

questions.q: Best initial nursing action for mild croup without stridor at rest is often:
options: Emergency intubation for every barky cough
Calm environment, supportive care, and escalation advice if worsening
questions.explanation: Mild croup is managed supportively with clear return precautions.

questions.q: A child with diabetes has ketones and glucose 22 mmol/L, is drinking and alert. The nurse anticipates:
options: Sick-day rules: insulin adjustment, fluids, frequent monitoring, and review if vomiting/drowsiness
questions.explanation: Hyperglycaemia with ketones needs structured sick-day management.

questions.q: Which play is most appropriate for a 2-year-old in hospital?
options: Parallel play with simple toys and caregiver involvement
questions.explanation: Toddlers engage in parallel play with simple exploration.

questions.q: A neonate of a diabetic mother is jittery at 2 hours of life. Priority is to:
options: Check blood glucose and treat hypoglycaemia per protocol
questions.explanation: IDM infants are at high risk of hypoglycaemia.

questions.q: Care of a child with a cast includes teaching families to report:
options: Foul smell, fever, or increasing pain/numbness of digits
Normal toe movement and pink colour
questions.explanation: Infection and neurovascular symptoms need urgent review.

questions.q: A child with HIV is admitted with pneumonia. Nursing priorities include:
options: Infection care, nutrition support, ART adherence support, and preventing opportunistic exposure as relevant
questions.explanation: Holistic HIV care includes medical treatment and confidentiality.

questions.q: Which assessment finding suggests moderate dehydration rather than mild?
options: Sunken eyes, reduced urine, lethargy or irritability, skin pinch slow
Normal tears and moist mucosa only
questions.explanation: Clinical scales distinguish some vs severe dehydration.

questions.q: A child has acute otitis media. Parent teaching includes:
options: Stopping antibiotics when pain improves at 24 hours always
Completing prescribed antibiotics if given, analgesia, and review if worsening
Inserting oil under pressure into the ear canal at home routinely
Swimming underwater during acute perforation pain without advice
questions.explanation: Analgesia and adherence matter; avoid harmful ear practices.

questions.q: Priority for a child with anaphylaxis after a drug is to:
options: Give oral antihistamine only and leave
IM adrenaline as protocol, airway support, call emergency help
Wait to see if symptoms pass for 30 minutes before acting
questions.explanation: IM adrenaline is first-line for anaphylaxis.

questions.q: A school child with epilepsy is seizing in the ward. After timing and safety, if the seizure continues beyond the protocol threshold the nurse prepares to:
options: Give oral tablets during active seizure
Administer prescribed rescue medication by the correct route
Restrain on the floor with a spoon in the mouth
Leave to find a relative first only
questions.explanation: Rescue medication is used for prolonged seizures per protocol.

questions.q: Which newborn screening discussion is accurate?
options: Early detection of selected conditions allows timely treatment; timing of the blood spot matters
Screening is optional paperwork with no health value
questions.explanation: Newborn screening enables early intervention when timed correctly.

questions.q: A child with severe malnutrition is started on feeds. The nurse watches closely for:
options: Refeeding complications (e.g. electrolyte shifts), tolerance, and fluid overload
Immediate high-protein adult diet on hour 1 always
Stopping all monitoring once the first sip is taken
questions.explanation: Refeeding must be careful and monitored.

questions.q: A toddler with a history of eczema has a severe flare with oozing and fever. Priority is to:
options: Assess for secondary infection and continue appropriate skin care / medical review
Use undiluted bleach baths daily without advice
questions.explanation: Infected eczema needs assessment and treatment.

questions.q: Which action reduces hospital-acquired infection in a paediatric ward?
options: Hand hygiene before and after every child contact
Using the same suction catheter on multiple children without cleaning
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene is the single most effective measure.

questions.q: A child in DKA has K+ 2.9 mmol/L before insulin is started. The nurse anticipates:
options: Potassium replacement planning with insulin as per protocol because insulin drives K+ intracellularly
questions.explanation: Hypokalaemia must be addressed carefully around insulin therapy.

questions.q: Best response when a parent is angry about waiting is to:
options: Stay calm, acknowledge concern, explain safety triage, and keep the child monitored
questions.explanation: De-escalation and clear communication maintain safety.

questions.q: A child with a Wilms tumour is being prepared for surgery. The nurse should avoid:
questions.explanation: Excessive palpation risks tumour rupture.

questions.q: Which sign indicates effective response to asthma treatment?
options: Improved air entry, reduced accessory muscle use, better saturations
questions.explanation: Clinical improvement guides response assessment.

questions.q: A 7-day-old with vomiting, lethargy and virilisation signs may need urgent evaluation for:
options: Possible congenital adrenal hyperplasia / salt-wasting crisis
questions.explanation: Salt-wasting CAH presents early with crisis risk.

questions.q: Home oxygen teaching is successful when caregivers state:
options: We increase flow freely without targets
We use the prescribed flow, monitor the child, and know emergency contacts / cylinder safety
We stop oxygen when the child is cyanosed
questions.explanation: Safety and prescribed use are essential.

questions.q: A child with acute diarrhoea is not dehydrated. The mainstay of care is:
options: Continued feeding, ORS for replacement of losses, zinc as protocol where recommended
questions.explanation: Feeding + ORS (± zinc) is standard for no dehydration.

questions.q: Which finding after ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion needs urgent reporting?
options: Bulging fontanelle, vomiting, irritability, or altered consciousness
questions.explanation: Signs of raised ICP or shunt failure need urgent review.

questions.q: A child with suspected meningitis is waiting for LP. The nurse prioritises:
options: Antibiotics without delay if indicated by protocol even if LP is deferred, plus monitoring
questions.explanation: Early antibiotics save lives when LP is delayed.

questions.q: Kawasaki disease concern is greatest regarding:
options: Only mild rash without systemic illness
Coronary artery complications — needs specialist treatment pathway (e.g. IVIG as ordered)
questions.explanation: Coronary involvement drives urgency of treatment.

questions.q: A child is on morphine PCA/NCA. RR falls to 8/min and is hard to rouse. Priority is to:
options: Support airway, oxygen, stop opioid, give naloxone as ordered
questions.explanation: Opioid depression needs reversal and airway support.

questions.q: Which toddler behaviour after hospitalisation is common and usually temporary?
questions.explanation: Regression under stress is common; support caregivers.

questions.q: A child with severe anaemia is pale and tachycardic. Nursing care while awaiting transfusion includes:
options: Minimise oxygen demand, monitor vitals, prepare for transfusion as ordered
questions.explanation: Reduce demand and prepare safe transfusion.

questions.q: Correct position for a child with gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms often includes:
options: Upright positioning after feeds as advised; smaller frequent feeds
Prone unsupervised sleep against safe-sleep guidance
questions.explanation: Upright posture and feed pattern changes help reflux symptoms.

questions.q: A neonate has respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen. The nurse suspects possible:
options: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia — avoid bag-mask if suspected, call advanced help
questions.explanation: CDH needs specialised airway management — avoid gut distension with bag-mask when suspected.

questions.q: Parent teaching for iron supplementation is correct when they say:
options: I give iron with milk only to improve absorption
I give as advised, may use vitamin C–containing fluids if recommended, and expect darker stools
Iron is unnecessary in complementary feeding age always
questions.explanation: Adherence and expected stool changes should be explained.

questions.q: A child with a central line has fever and redness at the exit site. Priority is to:
options: Report possible line infection — cultures/antibiotics per protocol
Use the line for routine blood draws without assessment
questions.explanation: Line infection risk requires prompt action.

questions.q: Which immunisation route teaching is accurate?
options: Route, site and age schedule matter; use the correct limb and technique
Any muscle is fine for any volume
Recap needles using two hands toward the body
questions.explanation: Correct route/site and sharps safety are essential.

questions.q: A child with acute asthma is on continuous nebulisers. Nursing priorities include:
options: Airway, saturations, work of breathing, and response to treatment
questions.explanation: Continuous assessment drives escalation.

questions.q: Suspected intussusception is a priority because:
options: Bowel ischaemia can develop — urgent diagnosis and reduction/surgery pathway
It is treated with high-fibre diet alone at home
questions.explanation: Time-critical bowel compromise risk.

questions.q: A child with burns has urine output of 0.2 mL/kg/h despite fluids. The nurse should:
options: Report — possible inadequate resuscitation or complications
questions.explanation: Urine output guides burn fluid resuscitation.

questions.q: Developmental dysplasia of the hip screening includes:
options: Ortolani/Barlow by trained staff and follow-up of risk factors
Encouraging tight swaddling with hips extended adducted
questions.explanation: Early detection prevents long-term disability.

questions.q: A child with pneumonia on antibiotics still has saturations 86% in air. Priority is to:
options: Stop oxygen thinking antibiotics are enough
Provide oxygen, reassess work of breathing, escalate
questions.explanation: Hypoxia needs oxygen regardless of antibiotic status.

questions.q: Which is a danger sign in a young infant under IMCI-style assessment?
options: Not feeding, convulsions, severe chest indrawing, or abnormally sleepy
questions.explanation: General danger signs require urgent referral/treatment.

questions.q: A child receiving chemotherapy vomits a dose of oral medication within 10 minutes. The nurse should:
options: Automatically double the next dose without orders
Follow protocol for re-dosing and antiemetic review; do not guess
Give IM injection of the same tablet
questions.explanation: Re-dosing rules are protocol-specific.

questions.q: Best practice when communicating with an adolescent about care is to:
options: Exclude them from all decisions always
Offer appropriate privacy and involve them in plans with consent/confidentiality limits explained
Speak only to parents in secret about everything without legal/ethical framework
questions.explanation: Respect and appropriate confidentiality support adherence.

questions.q: A child with severe dehydration is started on IV fluids. After 1 hour he is more alert but develops puffy eyelids. The nurse should:
options: Increase fluid rate further without review
Reassess for overhydration and report — adjust fluids as ordered
questions.explanation: Oedema during rehydration may signal excess fluid.

questions.q: Which action is appropriate for mild hypoglycaemia in a conscious child with diabetes?
options: 15 g fast carbohydrate, recheck glucose, then complex carb as protocol
questions.explanation: Rule of 15-style treatment for conscious hypoglycaemia.

questions.q: A child has a near-drowning event and is now breathing but drowsy. Priority is to:
options: ABC support, oxygen, temperature care, and hospital evaluation for delayed complications
Feed a large meal at the scene
No monitoring needed if coughing once
questions.explanation: Secondary drowning/aspiration risks need observation.

questions.q: Parent teaching for oral morphine at home (palliative) is correct when they say:
options: I save doses for when pain is unbearable only if prescribed regularly
I give doses on schedule for continuous pain and use breakthrough as prescribed
I stop if the child is sleepy without advice when pain is severe
questions.explanation: Regular dosing plus breakthrough is standard for continuous pain.

questions.q: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia has platelets 8 × 10⁹/L. Priority nursing includes:
options: Bleeding precautions and reporting headache/visual change (possible ICH)
questions.explanation: Severe thrombocytopenia → prevent and detect bleeding.

questions.q: Which statement about SIDS risk reduction is correct?
options: Prone sleep on soft pillows is safest
Supine sleep, firm surface, no smoke exposure, avoid overheating
Co-sleeping with soft duvet always recommended for all
Side sleep with loose blankets is ideal
questions.explanation: Back to sleep and safe sleep environment reduce SIDS risk.

questions.q: A child with suspected testicular torsion has sudden scrotal pain. The nurse should:
options: Apply ice and review next week
questions.explanation: Torsion is a surgical emergency.

questions.q: During peak flow teaching for an older child with asthma, success is shown when they:
options: Stand, seal lips, blow hard and fast, record best of three as taught
Share the meter mouthpiece without cleaning
Use peak flow only during sleep
questions.explanation: Correct technique yields useful readings.

questions.q: A malnourished child develops congestive findings after aggressive feeding. This most likely indicates:
options: Possible refeeding syndrome / fluid overload — urgent review
questions.explanation: Refeeding complications need immediate recognition.

questions.q: Which child needs droplet precautions?
options: Suspected meningococcal disease or influenza as per policy
questions.explanation: Certain respiratory/meningococcal illnesses need droplet precautions.

questions.q: A child has a Guedel airway in situ post-seizure. Nursing care includes:
options: Airway patency, positioning, and removal as consciousness returns per practice
questions.explanation: Airways are temporising until protective reflexes return.

questions.q: Priority teaching for caregivers of a child with a new permanent tracheostomy includes:
options: Suction, tube change emergency plan, and recognising obstruction
questions.explanation: Caregivers must manage airway emergencies.

questions.q: A child with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis should have which nursing focus?
options: High-salt snacks and free fluids always
BP monitoring, fluid balance, and activity as ordered
Stopping antibiotics if still prescribed without advice
questions.explanation: BP and fluid status drive complications risk.

questions.q: Which is the best indicator that ORS therapy is working?
options: Child becomes more alert and starts passing urine
questions.explanation: Clinical improvement and urine output show response.

questions.q: A child is receiving IV acyclovir for encephalitis. Nursing priorities include:
options: Hydration, renal function awareness, and neuro observations
questions.explanation: Acyclovir and encephalitis both need careful monitoring.

questions.q: A toddler refuses oral medication. The best approach is to:
options: Mix into a full bottle so the dose is uncertain
Use honest simple explanation, appropriate format, and caregiver help — avoid forcing into a fighting child without a plan
Hold the nose until they gasp every time as first line
Skip essential medicines without informing the team
questions.explanation: Developmental approach improves success and safety.

questions.q: A child with severe asthma has been given three bronchodilator treatments. Still distressed, saturations 91%. Next step is to:
options: Escalate to senior review / next-line therapy per protocol without delay
questions.explanation: Poor response requires escalation.

questions.q: Which newborn weight pattern is concerning by day 10?
options: Back to birth weight or above with good feeds
Still 12% below birth weight with poor urine output
questions.explanation: Failure to regain with oliguria needs assessment.

questions.q: A child with haemophilia needs dental extraction. Priority planning includes:
options: Haematology plan for factor replacement and bleeding risk minimisation
IM sedation in the cheek without plan
questions.explanation: Procedures need haematology-coordinated cover.

questions.q: Best initial measure for mild hypoglycaemia symptoms at school (conscious child) is:
options: Fast-acting sugar per plan, supervise, recheck as protocol
questions.explanation: Immediate carbohydrate is first-line if safe to swallow.

questions.q: A child has petechiae, fever, and headache. The nurse’s priority is to:
options: Urgent review for possible meningococcal disease / sepsis
questions.explanation: Fever + purpura is an emergency until proven otherwise.

questions.q: Which nursing action supports a child with chronic illness psychologically?
options: Excluding them from age-appropriate activities always
Encouraging normalised routines and honest communication
Avoiding all school contact permanently without need
questions.explanation: Normalisation and honesty support coping.

questions.q: A child with a chest drain: continuous bubbling in the water seal with respiratory distress may indicate:
options: Air leak — assess connections and escalate
Need to clamp permanently without orders
questions.explanation: Continuous bubbling can mean ongoing leak; assess and escalate.

questions.q: Priority in paediatric septic shock is to:
options: Delay antibiotics until all cultures return in 48 hours always
Oxygen, rapid fluid resuscitation as protocol, early antibiotics, and senior help
questions.explanation: Sepsis bundles prioritise oxygen, fluids, antibiotics and escalation.

questions.q: A child with acute otitis media and a bulging red tympanic membrane is in severe pain. Nursing priority includes:
options: Adequate analgesia and medical treatment plan
Swimming lesson same day if perforated and painful
questions.explanation: Pain control is essential alongside specific therapy.

questions.q: Which feeding advice is appropriate after cleft palate repair (as commonly ordered)?
options: Hard bottle nipples immediately against surgical advice
Follow surgical feeding protocol; protect the repair
Utensils that trauma the suture line
Unsupervised rough play with toys in the mouth day 1
questions.explanation: Protecting the repair is the feeding priority.

questions.q: A child with diabetes is sweating during sport. First action:
options: Give extra insulin immediately without checking
Check glucose if possible and treat hypo if indicated; take sugar if typical hypo symptoms
questions.explanation: Exercise-related hypo needs glucose check/treatment.

questions.q: Safe sleep counselling includes avoiding:
options: Soft bedding, prone sleep, and smoke exposure
questions.explanation: Soft bedding and prone sleep increase SIDS risk.

questions.q: A child with a known latex allergy needs:
options: Balloon play in the treatment room
questions.explanation: Avoidance and clear alerts prevent anaphylaxis.

questions.q: Which observation after head injury in a child needs urgent return to ED?
options: One episode of crying then normal play
Repeated vomiting, increasing drowsiness, or unequal pupils
Minor bump with immediate crying then normal behaviour
questions.explanation: Red flags for intracranial injury require urgent care.

questions.q: A child on long-term oxygen has saturations of 78% with increased work of breathing. Priority is to:
options: Follow escalation plan: check supply/connections, support breathing, emergency help
questions.explanation: Acute desaturation needs structured emergency response.

questions.q: Best nursing approach to medication error discovery is to:
options: Ensure child safety first, then report via formal system and inform as required
Alter the chart to hide doses
questions.explanation: Safety, honesty and formal reporting protect patients.

questions.q: A child with sickle cell disease should seek urgent care for:
options: Fever, severe pain not responding to home plan, neurological signs, or respiratory distress
One bruise after known trauma that is typical
questions.explanation: Fever and organ crises need urgent pathways.

questions.q: Which measure helps prevent vertical transmission topics that overlap paediatric follow-up?
options: Following national PMTCT infant testing and prophylaxis guidelines
questions.explanation: Paediatric HIV prevention follows national testing/prophylaxis schedules.

questions.q: A child with acute diarrhoea has blood in stool and high fever. The nurse should:
options: Assume viral only and avoid assessment
Assess dehydration and escalate — possible invasive diarrhoea needing specific evaluation
Give antimotility drugs routinely to all toddlers
questions.explanation: Bloody diarrhoea needs careful assessment and selective investigation/treatment.

questions.q: Priority airway support for a child with severe croup and fatigue is to:
options: Leave them alone in a noisy room
Urgent senior airway support — fatigue signals impending obstruction
Force examination with tongue depressor now
questions.explanation: Fatigue in upper airway obstruction is ominous.

questions.q: A caregiver asks why hand hygiene matters before neonatal care. The best answer is:
options: It is only for staff convenience
Newborns have immature immunity; hands are a major source of harmful microbes
It replaces the need for clean equipment
It is optional if gloves are worn sometimes
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene protects vulnerable neonates.
